prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 800 words of John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London. The reader is a general reader with no medical background.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.

text:
In the late summer of 1854, a terrible sickness struck the crowded Soho district of London. The disease was cholera, which causes violent vomiting and diarrhea and can kill a healthy person within a day or two. In just a few days, hundreds of people living near Broad Street were dead. Whole families were wiped out. Neighbors fled, shops closed, and the streets fell quiet.

At the time, almost everyone in authority believed cholera spread through bad air. They called it miasma, a poisonous mist rising from rotting rubbish, sewers and filth. The idea seemed sensible. The poorest districts were both the smelliest and the sickest. Doctors and officials urged people to burn tar, scrub the streets and avoid foul odors.

John Snow, a physician who lived nearby, did not believe it. He had been thinking about cholera for years. Snow noticed that the illness began with stomach trouble rather than with any problem of the lungs. If people were breathing poisoned air, he reasoned, why would the first symptoms appear in the gut? He suspected that people were swallowing something, some invisible agent in food or drink, and that it passed from one sick person to the next. Nobody had yet seen the germs responsible. Snow had no microscope image to prove his case. What he had was a habit of careful observation and a stubborn willingness to count.

When the outbreak exploded a few streets from his home, Snow saw a chance to test his idea. He began walking the neighborhood and asking questions. Where had the dead lived? What had they eaten and drunk? Which pump did they use for water? In those days most homes had no running water. People collected it from public pumps that drew from wells sunk into the ground.

Snow obtained the list of deaths recorded by the local registrar and began marking each address on a street map. The deaths clustered tightly around one spot, the water pump on Broad Street. The closer a household stood to that pump, the more likely it was to have suffered a death. The pattern was hard to ignore, but Snow knew that a map alone would not convince his skeptical colleagues. He needed to explain the exceptions.

So he went looking for them, and the exceptions proved his point. A workhouse not far from the pump housed hundreds of poor residents, yet very few of them died. Snow discovered that the workhouse had its own private well and did not depend on the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street also escaped almost untouched. The workers there were given free beer as part of their pay, and they seem to have rarely bothered with the pump. Beer had been boiled during brewing, which would have killed whatever was in the water, though no one understood that at the time.

Then came the most haunting case. A widow who lived far away in Hampstead had died of cholera, along with her niece. Snow learned that the woman had once lived in Soho and liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it delivered to her every day. Neither she nor her niece had been anywhere near the outbreak. They had simply drunk the water from the pump.

By the evening of September 7, Snow was confident enough to take his evidence to the local board of guardians, the officials who ran the parish. He urged them to act. The next day they agreed to remove the handle from the Broad Street pump, so that no one could draw water from it. The pump was disabled, and the outbreak soon faded.

It is tempting to say that removing the handle ended the epidemic, but the truth is more complicated. The outbreak had already begun to decline before the handle was taken away, partly because so many residents had fled or died. Snow himself admitted this. Even so, his work did not stand or fall on that single act.

The authorities were not quickly persuaded. A committee later examined the matter and rejected his water theory, still clinging to miasma. Yet a local clergyman named Henry Whitehead, who had begun as a skeptic, did his own investigation and uncovered the source. A baby had fallen ill with cholera in a house right beside the pump, and the family had washed its soiled cloths in a way that let waste leak into the old cesspool near the well. Dirty water had seeped into the supply. Snow's guess about the mechanism was right.

Snow died in 1858, before his ideas were widely accepted. Within a few decades, scientists identified the cholera germ and proved that contaminated water spreads the disease. Today Snow is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how disease moves through populations. His great lesson was simple. Gather the facts, map them, hunt for the cases that do not fit, and follow the evidence wherever it leads.
